sections.heading: What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?
paragraphs: A trade surplus happens when a country sells more goods and services to other countries than it buys from them. Imagine if you sold more of your cool craft projects than you bought from your friends; you’d have a surplus!

Conversely, a trade deficit occurs when a country buys more than it sells. A deficit isn’t always bad. Sometimes countries import things, because people want them or because they don’t make enough of certain products at home.
Let’s take a look at two fictional countries: Toylandia and Snackville. As the name indicates, Toylandia specializes in making toys and Snackville specializes in making snacks.

If Toylandia sells toys worth $100 million to Snackville but only buys snacks worth $70 million, it has a trade surplus of $30 million. Snackville, on the other hand, has a trade deficit of $30 million because it buys more than it sells.

Origin of the Words

“Surplus” comes from the Latin word “superplus,” meaning “more than what is needed,” while “deficit” comes from the Latin “deficere,” meaning “to fail” or “to lack.”

Trade happens when one country sells things to another country (called exports) and buys things from another country (called imports).

mainIdeaQuestion.title: Main Idea Question
mainIdeaQuestion.question: Which statement best summarizes the main idea of the article?
options: A trade deficit is always harmful for any country, so countries should stop buying imports from their trading partners.
By comparing how much money a country earns from exports and spends on imports, we can tell whether it has a trade surplus or a trade deficit, as shown by Toylandia and Snackville.
The Latin word "superplus" is the only reason countries trade food, toys, clothes, cars, and technology.
Toylandia and Snackville are real nations that compete to see which one can sell snacks worth $100 million.

feedback.correct: Correct! Option B brings together exports vs. imports, comparing money earned and spent to identify a trade surplus or trade deficit, and the Toylandia–Snackville example.
feedback.incorrect: Check all four parts of the article: the intro question, word origins, exports/imports comparison, and the fictional Toylandia–Snackville example.

mainIdeaQuestion.explanation:
Option A is incorrect (X): The article explicitly states, "A deficit isn’t always bad," and explains that countries import things people want or do not make enough of at home.
Option B is correct (O): It accurately summarizes the whole article—defining exports (sells) and imports (buys), comparing money earned vs. spent to tell surplus from deficit, and illustrating both with Toylandia and Snackville.
Option C is incorrect (X): "Origin of the Words" explains where "trade," "surplus," and "deficit" come from, not why countries trade.
Option D is incorrect (X): The article states Toylandia and Snackville are "two fictional countries," and Toylandia sells toys worth $100 million while Snackville makes snacks.

questions.question: In the section "What Is Trade?", how are exports and imports defined?
options: Exports are things a country buys, and imports are things a country sells.
Exports are things a country sells, and imports are things a country buys.

Option A is incorrect (X): This swaps the two definitions.

questions.question: According to "What Is Trade?", how does a country determine whether it has a trade surplus or a trade deficit?

languageFocus.title: Language Focus
languageFocus.topic: Comparison, Contrast, Cause/Effect, Parentheses, Quantifiers & Economic Vocabulary
languageFocus.instructions: Study these 6 key grammar and language patterns from the article before completing Writing Practice and the Writing Task.

patterns.name: 1. Comparison (more ... than)
patterns.explanation: Use "more + noun/noun phrase + than" or "more than" to compare how much a country sells and buys when identifying a surplus or deficit.
patterns.example: A country has a trade surplus when it sells more goods and services than it buys.
patterns.sourceExample: A trade surplus happens when a country sells more goods and services to other countries than it buys from them.

patterns.name: 2. Contrast (Conversely, while, on the other hand, but)
patterns.explanation: Use contrast words to show opposite sides of trade: "Conversely," starts a contrasting sentence, "while" joins contrasting clauses, and "on the other hand" highlights the partner country’s opposite balance.
patterns.example: Toylandia has a $30 million trade surplus; conversely, Snackville has a $30 million trade deficit.
patterns.sourceExample: Conversely, a trade deficit occurs when a country buys more than it sells. / Snackville, on the other hand, has a trade deficit of $30 million...

patterns.name: 3. Cause and Effect (because, happens when, occurs when, tells us whether)
patterns.explanation: Use "because" to give reasons why countries import or why a deficit occurs, and use "happens when" / "occurs when" to explain what creates a surplus or deficit.
patterns.example: Snackville has a trade deficit because it buys more than it sells.
patterns.sourceExample: Sometimes countries import things, because people want them or because they don’t make enough of certain products at home. / ...because it buys more than it sells.

patterns.name: 4. Parentheses for Definitions ((called exports), (called imports))
patterns.explanation: Parentheses smoothly insert a short technical term right after its everyday explanation so readers learn economic terms in context.
patterns.example: When a country sells products abroad (called exports), it earns money from trade.
patterns.sourceExample: Trade happens when one country sells things to another country (called exports) and buys things from another country (called imports).

patterns.name: 5. Quantifiers & Exact Dollar Amounts (more, only, enough, $100M / $70M / $30M)
patterns.explanation: Quantifiers like "more," "only," and "enough" show relative size, while exact dollar figures ("$100 million," "$70 million," "$30 million") prove the arithmetic difference ($100M − $70M = $30M).
patterns.example: Toylandia earns $100 million from exports and spends only $70 million on imports, creating a $30 million surplus.
patterns.sourceExample: If Toylandia sells toys worth $100 million to Snackville but only buys snacks worth $70 million, it has a trade surplus of $30 million.

patterns.name: 6. Economic Vocabulary & Source Attribution
patterns.explanation: Use accurate lesson terms (trade, goods, services, exports, imports, surplus, deficit, specializes, at home) and attribute facts with "According to the article," while keeping Toylandia and Snackville fictional.
patterns.example: According to the article, countries compare money earned from exports and spent on imports to find a surplus or deficit.
patterns.sourceExample: Let’s take a look at two fictional countries: Toylandia and Snackville.

writingTask.modelAnswer: According to the article, exports are things a country sells to other countries, while imports are things a country buys from them. Countries keep track of how much money they earn from exports and spend on imports, and comparing these two numbers shows whether they have a trade surplus or a trade deficit. A trade surplus happens when a country sells more goods and services than it buys. Conversely, a trade deficit occurs when a country buys more than it sells, often because people want certain products or do not make enough at home. teacherNotes.topic: 1. Lesson Flow: Origins → Trade → Imports/Exports → Comparison → Surplus/Deficit → Fictional Amounts

teacherNotes.topic: 2. Deficit Is Not Always Bad Here
teacherNotes.note: Emphasize the article’s balanced statement: "A deficit isn’t always bad." Guide students to cite the exact two reasons given in the text: people want imported things, or countries do not make enough of certain products at home.

teacherNotes.topic: 3. Keep Toylandia & Snackville Fictional — No Macro Judgment
teacherNotes.note: Treat Toylandia and Snackville strictly as fictional teaching countries illustrating $100 million − $70 million = $30 million. Do not introduce outside macroeconomic topics (exchange rates, tariffs, GDP, debt, real-world country balances, or normative winners/losers judgments beyond the text).

teacherNotes.topic: 4. Two Ordered Source Images & Exact Text Preservation
teacherNotes.note: Any diagrams or maps in the two teacher-provided classroom source images are visual context only; never reconstruct visual-only labels as canonical prose. Preserve exact diacritic "trāde", curly quotes/apostrophes ("That’s", "isn’t", "don’t", "you’d", "Let’s"), lowercase "is" in "What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?", and exact dollar figures ($100 million, $70 million, $30 million).

teachingScript.objective: Introduce the Unit 3 global-trade topic, exact title, and source-only evidence rule.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Greet students, display the exact title and outside source attribution, and explain that diagrams/maps in classroom images are visual context only while answers must come from the canonical text.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Good morning, everyone! / Today we begin a Unit 3 economics reading: / "Trade Surplus & Deficit: / Understanding How Countries Buy and Sell." / Notice the two words / "surplus" and "deficit." / As we read the two source pages, / remember our key rule: / diagrams and maps are visual context only, / and every answer must come / directly from the wording in the article.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 안녕하세요 여러분! 오늘은 Unit 3 경제 읽기 지문 "Trade Surplus & Deficit: Understanding How Countries Buy and Sell"을 함께 읽습니다. "surplus(흑자)"와 "deficit(적자)"라는 두 단어에 주목하세요. 두 페이지의 자료를 읽을 때 꼭 기억할 규칙이 있습니다. 도표나 지도는 시각적 이해를 돕는 용도이며, 모든 답은 반드시 본문의 정확한 문장에서 찾아야 합니다.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students read the title, Unit 3 goal, and outside attribution (G1: identify the key words "buy," "sell," "surplus," and "deficit"; G2: predict what "winning or losing in trade" might refer to).
teachingScript.misconception: Assuming "winning or losing in trade" means a real-world trade war or bringing in outside economic terms like tariffs or GDP.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Clarify that the article answers this simply by comparing exports and imports and keeping the Toylandia–Snackville example purely fictional (G1: point to "buy and sell" in the title; G2: note we stay inside the text without outside macroeconomics).
teachingScript.transition: Before reading, let us activate our everyday ideas with three warm-up questions.

teachingScript.objective: Activate everyday ideas about buying/selling, exports/imports, and selling more than buying.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Guide pairs through Warm-up Q1–Q3 using sentence starters and elicit brief oral and written responses.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Let us look at Warm-up Question 1: / What everyday things do countries buy and sell? / Next, Question 2: / How is selling to another country / different from buying from another country? / Finally, Question 3: / If you sold more craft projects / than you bought from friends, / would you have extra money or less money?
teachingScript.scriptKo: 워밍업 1번 질문을 봅시다. 나라들은 일상에서 어떤 물건들을 사고파나요? 2번은 다른 나라에 파는 것과 사오는 것의 차이입니다. 3번은 친구들에게서 산 것보다 공예품을 더 많이 팔았을 때 돈이 남는지 생각해 보는 질문입니다.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students discuss in pairs and write 1–2 sentences per question (G1: complete the provided starters; G2: give a concrete example of buying vs. selling and explain why extra money remains).
teachingScript.misconception: Confusing "import" (buying in) with "export" (selling out) or saying buying more leaves extra money.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Use the prefix clue: ex- = out (sell out), im- = in (buy in), and remind students that selling more brings more money in than goes out (G1: match "export = sell", "import = buy"; G2: explain the direction of goods and money).
teachingScript.transition: Now let us read the exact article across both source pages in order.

teachingScript.objective: Read the intro, 3 section headings, 2 bullets, and all 18 sentences in order while separating visual diagrams/maps from text.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Read Image 1 and Image 2 aloud with slash pauses; check the flow from origins → trade → imports/exports → comparison → surplus/deficit → Toylandia/Snackville ($100M/$70M/$30M).

teachingScript.scriptKo: 글의 흐름을 차례대로 따라가 봅시다. 먼저 도입부는 한 나라가 무역에서 이기고 있는지 지고 있는지 어떻게 알 수 있는지 묻습니다. 다음 "Origin of the Words"는 trāde, superplus, deficere의 어원을 설명하고, "What Is Trade?"는 수출과 수입을 정의한 뒤 번 돈과 쓴 돈을 비교합니다. 마지막 "What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?"에서는 두 개념과 적자가 항상 나쁜 것은 아닌 이유, 그리고 Toylandia와 Snackville 예시를 살펴봅니다.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students track headings, underline "(called exports)" and "(called imports)", and verify the $100M − $70M = $30M subtraction (G1: highlight Exports = sells, Imports = buys, and the three dollar numbers; G2: trace the transition from word origins to the fictional numbers).
teachingScript.misconception: Treating Toylandia and Snackville as real countries or judging a trade deficit as automatically bad.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Point directly to "two fictional countries" and "A deficit isn’t always bad" (G1: circle "fictional" and "isn’t always bad"; G2: list the two "because" reasons given in the text).
teachingScript.transition: Now let us study all 10 target vocabulary items from the reading.

teachingScript.objective: Master all 10 exact vocabulary items with definitions, Korean meanings, source quotes, and student examples.
teachingScript.teacherActions: Review pronunciation, word forms, and context for trade, goods, services, exports, imports, surplus, deficit, conversely, specializes, and at home.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Check our ten vocabulary cards. / Group "trade," "goods," and "services" first: / trade means buying and selling goods and services. / Next, pair "exports" and "imports," / then "surplus" and "deficit." / Notice "conversely" signals the opposite case, / "specializes" means focusing on one product, / and "at home" means inside one’s own country.

teachingScript.misconception: Thinking "at home" means inside a student’s house rather than inside one’s own country.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Explain that in economics texts like this one, "at home" means domestically inside the country (G1: note Korean "자국 내에서"; G2: contrast "at home" with "other countries").

warmUpTeacherGuide.question: What everyday items like food, toys, clothes, or technology do people or countries buy and sell with one another?
warmUpTeacherGuide.focus: Activating everyday goods traded between countries
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherTalk: Think about what you ate, / wore, or used today. / Which everyday items / do countries buy and sell / around the world?
warmUpTeacherGuide.korean: 오늘 먹거나 입거나 사용한 물건을 떠올려 보세요. 세계 여러 나라는 어떤 일상 물품을 사고파나요?
warmUpTeacherGuide.sampleAnswer: Countries and people often buy and sell everyday things like food, clothes, toys, cars, and phones.
likelyResponses: Countries trade food, clothes, cars, and electronics.
People buy snacks and toys made in other places.
warmUpTeacherGuide.followUp: Notice in the opening sentence which five examples the article names.
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherFollowUpKorean: 도입부 첫 문장에서 글이 어떤 다섯 가지 예시를 드는지 확인해 보세요.
warmUpTeacherGuide.caution: Keep examples simple and everyday; avoid real-world trade disputes.
warmUpTeacherGuide.purpose: Prepare students for Paragraph 1’s trade examples.

warmUpTeacherGuide.question: In your own words, what is the difference between a country selling products to another country (export) and buying products from another country (import)?
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherTalk: Look at the two prefixes: / ex- means out, / and im- means in. / When a country sends goods out to sell, / what is that called? / And when it brings goods in to buy?
warmUpTeacherGuide.korean: 두 접두사를 보세요. ex-는 밖으로, im-은 안으로를 뜻합니다. 물건을 밖으로 내보내 판는 것과 안으로 들여와 사는 것은 어떻게 다를까요?
warmUpTeacherGuide.sampleAnswer: Selling products to another country means exporting and earning money, while buying products from another country means importing and spending money.
likelyResponses: Exports go out to other countries, and imports come in.
Exports earn money and imports cost money.
warmUpTeacherGuide.followUp: Check the two bullet points under "What Is Trade?" to verify the exact short definitions.
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherFollowUpKorean: "What Is Trade?" 아래 두 개의 불릿 포인트에서 짧은 정의를 확인해 보세요.
warmUpTeacherGuide.caution: Prevent students from reversing sell/buy on exports and imports.
warmUpTeacherGuide.purpose: Anchor exports vs. imports before reading.

warmUpTeacherGuide.question: Imagine you sold more craft projects than you bought from friends. Would you end up with extra money or less money, and why?
warmUpTeacherGuide.focus: Intuitive grasp of "more sold than bought" (surplus vs. deficit)
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherTalk: Imagine a class craft fair. / If you sell more craft projects / than you buy from friends, / do you earn more money than you spend? / What if you buy more than you sell?
warmUpTeacherGuide.korean: 반 공예품 장터를 상상해 보세요. 친구에게서 산 것보다 더 많이 팔았다면 쓴 돈보다 번 돈이 더 많을까요? 반대로 판 것보다 더 많이 샀다면 어떨까요?
warmUpTeacherGuide.sampleAnswer: If I sold more craft projects than I bought, I would have extra money because I earned more than I spent.
likelyResponses: I would have extra money because selling brings money in.
If I bought more than I sold, I would spend more than I earned.
warmUpTeacherGuide.followUp: Look for that exact craft-project analogy in "What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?".
warmUpTeacherGuide.teacherFollowUpKorean: "What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?" 문단에서 바로 그 공예품 비유를 찾아보세요.
warmUpTeacherGuide.caution: Keep focus on comparing money earned vs. money spent, not personal moral judgment.
warmUpTeacherGuide.purpose: Prime students for the craft-projects analogy and Toylandia–Snackville math.

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Buying and selling between countries.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Every day, countries around the world trade things like food, toys, clothes, cars, and even technology.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Every day, / countries around the world / trade things / like food, toys, clothes, cars, / and even technology.

sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 매일 전 세계 나라들은 음식, 장난감, 옷, 자동차, 심지어 기술 제품까지 다양한 것들을 교역한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 띄어 쓴 Every day는 "매일"이라는 시간 부사구이고, 붙여 쓴 everyday는 "일상의"라는 형용사입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 시간 부사구 Every day가 문두에 오고 복수 주어(countries around the world)에 현재시제 동사 trade("교역하다")가 이어집니다. 전치사 like 뒤에 5개 명사가 병렬 나열되었습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Trade happens all the time / around the entire world. / Countries buy and sell / everyday items like food, toys, and clothes. / They also trade bigger items / like cars and even technology.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 무역은 전 세계에서 늘 일어납니다. 나라들은 음식, 장난감, 옷 같은 일상 물품을 사고팝니다. 자동차나 심지어 기술 제품 같은 더 큰 물건들도 거래합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Is "trade" a noun or a verb in this sentence, and what five examples follow "like"?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 이 문장에서 "trade"는 명사인가요 동사인가요? 그리고 "like" 뒤에 나오는 다섯 가지 예시는 무엇인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: It is a verb ("countries ... trade"), and the five examples are food, toys, clothes, cars, and technology.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 동사("countries ... trade")이고, 다섯 가지 예시는 food, toys, clothes, cars, technology입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: But how do we know if a country is winning or losing in trade?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: But / how do we know / if a country is winning or losing / in trade?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 하지만 / 우리는 어떻게 알 수 있을까 / 한 나라가 이기고 있는지 지고 있는지 / 무역에서?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 하지만 한 나라가 무역에서 이기고 있는지 지고 있는지를 우리는 어떻게 알 수 있을까?

mustKnowChunks.use: 접속사 if는 "~인지 아닌지"(whether)를 뜻하는 명사절을 이끌어 know의 목적어 역할을 합니다.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 의문사 how + do + 주어(we) + 동사원형(know) 의문문 뒤에 명사절 접속사 if("~인지") + 현재진행형(is winning or losing)이 왔습니다. 여기서 if는 조건("~라면")이 아니라 "~인지"입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Everyone trades, / so a natural question comes up. / How can we tell / whether a country is ahead or behind? / This question hooks the reader / before introducing two key terms.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 모든 나라가 무역을 하니 자연스러운 질문이 생깁니다. 한 나라가 앞서고 있는지 뒤처지고 있는지 어떻게 알 수 있을까요? 이 질문은 두 핵심 용어를 소개하기 전에 독자의 관심을 끌어 당깁니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Does "if" mean "on the condition that" or "whether" in "know if a country is winning or losing"?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "know if a country is winning or losing"에서 "if"는 "만약 ~라면"인가요, "~인지 아닌지(whether)"인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: It means "whether," introducing the noun clause after "know."
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "know" 뒤에 오는 명사절을 이끄는 "~인지(whether)"라는 뜻입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: What two ideas does the colon introduce after "come in"?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Trade surplus and trade deficit.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 무역 흑자(trade surplus)와 무역 적자(trade deficit)입니다.

teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "why they matter"에서 동사 "matter"는 무슨 뜻인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: It means "are important."
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "중요하다"라는 뜻입니다.

teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 원래 "길, 경로, 발자국"을 뜻했고, 나중에는 재화와 서비스를 사고파는 과정을 뜻하게 되었습니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: “Surplus” comes from the Latin word “superplus,” meaning “more than what is needed,” while “deficit” comes from the Latin “deficere,” meaning “to fail” or “to lack.”
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: “Surplus” comes from / the Latin word “superplus,” / meaning “more than what is needed,” / while “deficit” comes from / the Latin “deficere,” / meaning “to fail” or “to lack.”
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: "Surplus"는 ~에서 왔다 / 라틴어 단어 "superplus"에서, / "필요한 것보다 더 많은"을 뜻하는, / 반면 "deficit"은 ~에서 왔다 / 라틴어 "deficere"에서, / "부족하다"나 "모자라다"를 뜻하는.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: "Surplus"는 "필요한 것보다 더 많은"을 뜻하는 라틴어 "superplus"에서 왔으며, 반면 "deficit"은 "실패하다" 또는 "부족하다"를 뜻하는 라틴어 "deficere"에서 유래했다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 두 대상("Surplus"와 "deficit")의 차이를 한 문장 안에서 대조할 때 쓰는 접속사입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Toylandia has a surplus, while Snackville has a deficit.

mustKnowChunks.use: 선행사를 포함한 관계대명사 what(~하는 것)이 쓰였습니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: A surplus means having more than what is needed.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 대조 접속사 while("~인 반면에")이 두 절을 연결합니다. 각 절 끝의 분사구문(meaning “more than what is needed,” / meaning “to fail” or “to lack.”)이 라틴어 단어 superplus와 deficere를 대칭적으로 풀어 줍니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now we learn the Latin roots / of our two main terms. / "Surplus" comes from "superplus," / meaning extra or more than needed. / Meanwhile, / "deficit" comes from "deficere," / meaning to lack or fall short.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 두 핵심 용어의 라틴어 어원을 배웁니다. "Surplus"는 필요한 것보다 더 많음을 뜻하는 "superplus"에서 왔습니다. 반면 "deficit"은 모자라고 부족함을 뜻하는 "deficere"에서 왔습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Which word connects to "more than what is needed," and how does "while" link the two clauses?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 어떤 단어가 "필요한 것보다 더 많은"과 연결되며, "while"은 두 절을 어떻게 이어 주나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: "Surplus" ("superplus") connects to more than needed, and "while" contrasts it with "deficit" ("deficere").
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "Surplus"("superplus")가 필요 이상을 뜻하고, "while"이 그것을 "deficit"("deficere")와 대조해 줍니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: What Is Trade?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: What / Is Trade?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 무엇인가 / 무역은?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 무역이란 무엇인가?

mustKnowChunks.use: 질문형 소제목으로 정의와 핵심 구성 요소(수출·수입)를 이끌어 냅니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Under "What Is Trade?", the text defines exports and imports.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 의문사 What + be동사 Is + 주어 Trade? 형태의 제목입니다. (Is의 대문자 표기는 원문 그대로 유지합니다.)
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now that we know the word origins, / this heading asks a simple question. / What is trade? / The next lines will break trade / into two clear actions: selling and buying.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 단어의 어원을 알았으니 이 제목은 간단한 질문을 던집니다. 무역이란 무엇일까요? 이어지는 문장들은 무역을 팔기와 사기라는 두 가지 명확한 행동으로 나누어 설명합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: What two terms will answer "What Is Trade?" right below this heading?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 이 제목 바래 아래에서 "What Is Trade?"에 답하는 두 가지 용어는 무엇인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Exports and imports.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 수출(exports)과 수입(imports)입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Trade happens when one country sells things to another country (called exports) and buys things from another country (called imports).
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Trade happens / when one country sells things to another country / (called exports) / and buys things from another country / (called imports).
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 무역은 일어난다 / 한 나라가 다른 나라에 물건을 팔 때 / (수출이라고 불리는) / 그리고 다른 나라로부터 물건을 살 때 / (수입이라고 불리는).
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 무역은 한 나라가 다른 나라에 물건을 팔고(수출), 다른 나라로부터 물건을 살 때(수입) 일어난다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 괄호 안의 과거분사 called + 명사는 앞 내용의 전문 용어를 짧게 붙여 주는 동격 설명입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Countries sell goods abroad (called exports) and buy goods from abroad (called imports).

mustKnowChunks.chunk: sells things to ~ / buys things from ~
mustKnowChunks.use: sell A to B(팔는 방향 to) vs. buy A from B(사오는 출처 from) 전치사 대비에 주의합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Toylandia sells toys to Snackville and buys snacks from Snackville.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 시간 접속사 when절 안에서 단수 주어 one country에 맞춘 두 동사 sells와 buys가 and로 병렬 연결되었습니다. 괄호 안의 (called exports)와 (called imports)는 각각 정의를 보충합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Trade is simply two-way buying and selling / between countries. / When a country sends goods out to sell, / we call those "exports." / When it buys goods from elsewhere, / we call those "imports."
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 무역은 나라들 사이에서 일어나는 양방향 사고팔기입니다. 한 나라가 물건을 밖으로 내보내 팔 때 그것을 "수출(exports)"이라 부르고, 다른 나라에서 사올 때 "수입(imports)"이라 부릅니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Why does the writer put "(called exports)" and "(called imports)" in parentheses?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 글쓴이가 왜 "(called exports)"와 "(called imports)"를 괄호 안에 넣었을까요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: To give the exact terms right after explaining "sells things" and "buys things."
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "물건을 판다"와 "물건을 산다"를 설명한 바로 뒤에 정확한 용어를 알려 주기 위해서입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Exports = things a country sells
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Exports / = things a country sells
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 수출 / = 한 나라가 파는 것들
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 수출 = 한 나라가 파는 물건들

mustKnowChunks.use: things (that) a country sells에서 목적격 관계대명사 that이 생략되어 명사 things를 수식합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Toys are things Toylandia sells to Snackville.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 등호(=)를 사용한 간결한 불릿 정의입니다. things 뒤에 목적격 관계대명사 that/which가 생략된 수식절(a country sells)가 왔습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: This bullet point is a quick memory card. / Keep it simple: / Exports = things going out / that a country sells. / Picture the "ex-" in "exit."
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이 불릿 포인트는 한눈에 외우는 요약 카드입니다. 간단하게 기억하세요. Exports = 나라가 밖으로 파는 것들입니다. "exit(출구)"의 "ex-"를 떠올리세요.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: In six short words, what does the first bullet define?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 첫 번째 불릿 포인트는 무엇을 간단히 정의하나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Exports = things a country sells.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: Exports = 한 나라가 파는 것들입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Imports = things a country buys
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Imports / = things a country buys
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 수입 / = 한 나라가 사는 것들
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 수입 = 한 나라가 사오는 물건들

mustKnowChunks.use: things (that) a country buys 구조로, 단수 주어 a country에 -s(buys)를 붙입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Snacks are things Toylandia buys from Snackville.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 첫 번째 불릿과 완벽한 대구를 이루는 등호(=) 정의입니다. 목적격 관계대명사 생략 구조(things a country buys)이며 buys의 3인칭 단수 -s를 유지합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: This second bullet gives the opposite side. / Imports = things coming in / that a country buys. / Picture the "im-" as "in," / bringing products into the country.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 두 번째 불릿은 반대쪽 개념을 알려 줍니다. Imports = 나라 안으로 사들여오는 것들입니다. "im-"을 "in(안으로)"으로 떠올리세요.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: How do the two bullets help us keep exports and imports straight?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 두 불릿 포인트가 수출과 수입을 헷갈리지 않도록 어떻게 도와주나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: They give a short side-by-side rule: Exports = sells, Imports = buys.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: Exports = 파는 것, Imports = 사는 것이라는 짧은 대조 규칙을 보여 줍니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: A country keeps track of how much money it earns from exports and how much it spends on imports.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: A country keeps track of / how much money it earns from exports / and how much it spends on imports.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 한 나라는 기록하며 추적한다 / 수출로 얼마나 많은 돈을 버는지 / 그리고 수입에 얼마나 많이 쓰는지.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 한 나라는 수출을 통해 얼마의 돈을 벌고 수입에 얼마를 쓰는지 기록한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 숫자나 금액을 빠뜨리지 않고 계산·추적할 때 쓰는 관용 표현입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: A country keeps track of money earned and spent.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: earns from exports / spends on imports
mustKnowChunks.use: earn money from ~ / spend money on ~ 전치사 호응에 주의하세요.
mustKnowChunks.example: Toylandia earns $100 million from exports and spends $70 million on imports.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: keeps track of 뒤에 두 개의 간접의문문(how much money it earns from exports / how much it spends on imports)이 and로 연결되었습니다. 두 번째 how much 뒤에는 money가 생략되었습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Next, / countries count the money. / They watch two numbers carefully. / One is money earned from selling exports, / and the other is money spent on buying imports.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 다음으로 나라들은 돈을 셉니다. 두 가지 숫자를 꼼꼼히 살핍니다. 하나는 수출을 팔아 번 돈이고, 다른 하나는 수입을 사는 데 쓴 돈입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Which prepositions pair with "earns" and "spends" here?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 여기서 "earns"와 "spends"는 각각 어떤 전치사와 짝을 이루나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: "Earns from" exports, and "spends on" imports.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "earns from" exports, 그리고 "spends on" imports입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Comparing these two numbers tells us whether the country has a trade surplus or a trade deficit.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Comparing these two numbers / tells us / whether the country has / a trade surplus or a trade deficit.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 이 두 숫자를 비교하는 것은 / 우리에게 알려 준다 / 그 나라가 가졌는지 / 무역 흑자를 또는 무역 적자를.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 이 두 숫자를 비교하면 그 나라가 무역 흑자인지 무역 적자인지 알 수 있다.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: Comparing these two numbers tells us whether ~
mustKnowChunks.meaning: 이 두 숫자를 비교하는 것은 ~인지 알려 준다
mustKnowChunks.use: 동명사 주어(Comparing...) + 단수 동사(tells) + whether A or B 구조입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Comparing exports and imports tells us whether trade is in surplus or deficit.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 동명사구 주어 Comparing these two numbers는 단수 취급하여 tells(-s)를 쓰고, 간접목적어 us 뒤에 whether ~ or ~ 명사절이 직접목적어로 옵니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Once you have both numbers, / put them side by side. / Compare money earned / with money spent. / That comparison immediately shows / whether the country has a surplus or a deficit.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 두 숫자를 모두 구했다면 나란히 놓고 비교해 보세요. 번 돈과 쓴 돈을 비교하면 그 나라가 흑자인지 적자인지 바로 알 수 있습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Why does "tells" end in -s here even though "numbers" is plural?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "numbers"가 복수인데도 왜 동사 "tells"에 -s가 붙었나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Because the subject is the singular gerund phrase "Comparing these two numbers."
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 주어가 단수 취급하는 동명사구 "Comparing these two numbers"이기 때문입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: What / is Trade Surplus and Deficit?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 무엇인가 / 무역 흑자와 적자는?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 무역 흑자와 적자란 무엇인가?

mustKnowChunks.chunk: What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?
mustKnowChunks.use: 소문자 is 표기를 포함해 원문 제목 그대로 두 개념의 정의와 예시를 열어 줍니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: In "What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?", the article compares both terms.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: Trade Surplus and Deficit을 하나의 묶음 주제로 보아 단수 동사 is를 쓴 섹션 제목입니다. (소문자 is 철자 원문 그대로 보존)
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now we move to Page 2. / This heading asks for exact meanings: / what is a trade surplus, / and what is a trade deficit? / Next, / we will see both definitions, / a craft analogy, / and a fictional country example.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 2페이지로 넘어갑니다. 이 제목은 무역 흑자와 무역 적자의 정확한 뜻을 묻습니다. 이어서 두 정의와 공예품 비유, 그리고 가상 국가 예시를 보게 됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Look at the capitalization in "What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?" compared to "What Is Trade?".
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "What Is Trade?"와 "What is Trade Surplus and Deficit?"의 대소문자 표기를 비교해 보세요.

teachingTranscript.english: Student: The second heading uses lowercase "is," and we preserve the source spelling exactly.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 두 번째 제목은 소문자 "is"를 쓰며, 우리는 원문 표기를 그대로 유지합니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: A trade surplus happens when a country sells more goods and services to other countries than it buys from them.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: A trade surplus happens / when a country sells more goods and services / to other countries / than it buys from them.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 무역 흑자는 일어난다 / 한 나라가 더 많은 재화와 서비스를 팔 때 / 다른 나라들에게 / 그들로부터 사는 것보다.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 무역 흑자는 한 나라가 다른 나라들로부터 사는 것보다 더 많은 재화와 서비스를 팔 때 발생한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: more + 명사 + than ~ 비교 구문으로 흑자의 핵심 조건(판매 > 구매)을 정의합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: A surplus happens when a country sells more than it buys.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: happens when 조건·시간 접속사 뒤에 비교구문 more goods and services ... than it buys from them이 왔습니다. 대명사 it은 a country를, them은 other countries를 가리킵니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Here is the simple rule / for a trade surplus. / Exports are bigger than imports. / A country sells more goods and services / to other countries / than it buys from them.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 무역 흑자의 간단한 규칙이 있습니다. 수출이 수입보다 더 큽니다. 한 나라가 다른 나라들로부터 사는 것보다 다른 나라들에 파는 재화와 서비스가 더 많습니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: What do "it" and "them" refer back to in "than it buys from them"?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "than it buys from them"에서 "it"과 "them"은 각각 무엇을 가리키나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: "It" refers to "a country," and "them" refers to "other countries."
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "it"은 "a country"를, "them"은 "other countries"를 가리킵니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Imagine if you sold more of your cool craft projects than you bought from your friends; you’d have a surplus!
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Imagine if you sold / more of your cool craft projects / than you bought from your friends; / you’d have a surplus!
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 상상해 보라 / 네가 더 많은 멋진 공예품을 팔았다면 / 친구들에게서 산 것보다; / 너는 흑자를 갖게 될 것이다!
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 친구들에게서 산 것보다 네 멋진 공예품을 더 많이 팔았다고 상상해 보자. 그러면 너에겐 흑자가 생긴다!

mustKnowChunks.chunk: Imagine if you sold ~; you’d have ~
mustKnowChunks.meaning: 네가 ~했다고 상상해 보자; 너는 ~을 갖게 될 것이다
mustKnowChunks.use: 가정법 과거(sold / bought → you’d = you would)로 일상 비유를 만듭니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Imagine if you earned more than you spent; you’d have extra money!

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 명령문 Imagine + 가정법 if절(sold ... bought) 뒤에 세미콜론(;)이 오고, 주절 you’d(you would) have a surplus!가 결과를 보여 줍니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: To make this easy to picture, / think about friends trading crafts. / Suppose you sell more craft items / than you buy from friends. / Because more money comes in than goes out, / you end up with a surplus!
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이해하기 쉽게 친구들과 공예품을 사고파는 상황을 떠올려 보세요. 친구에게서 산 것보다 더 많은 공예품을 판다면, 나간 돈보다 들어온 돈이 많아 흑자가 생깁니다!

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: What two words does "you’d" stand for here, and why does the sentence use past tense "sold" and "bought"?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 여기서 "you’d"는 무엇의 줄임말이며, 왜 과거형 "sold"와 "bought"를 썼나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: "You’d" stands for "you would," and past forms mark an imaginary "Imagine if" scenario.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: "you’d"는 "you would"의 줄임말이고, "Imagine if" 가정 상황을 나타내기 위해 과거형을 썼습니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Conversely, a trade deficit occurs when a country buys more than it sells.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Conversely, / a trade deficit occurs / when a country buys more / than it sells.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 반대로, / 무역 적자는 발생한다 / 한 나라가 더 많이 살 때 / 파는 것보다.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 반대로 무역 적자는 한 나라가 파는 것보다 더 많이 살 때 발생한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 문두 부사 Conversely는 앞 문단(흑자)의 정반대 개념(적자)을 도입합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Conversely, a trade deficit occurs when imports exceed exports.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 연결부사 Conversely로 전환하고 단수 주어(a trade deficit) + 단수 동사(occurs) + when 부사절(buys more than it sells)로 흑자 정의와 대칭을 이루었습니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now flip the direction around. / "Conversely" tells us / the opposite case is coming. / A trade deficit happens / when a country buys more / than it sells.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 방향을 반대로 뒤집어 봅시다. "Conversely"는 반대 상황이 나온다는 신호입니다. 무역 적자는 한 나라가 파는 것보다 더 많이 살 때 일어납니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Why does the writer start this paragraph with "Conversely,"?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 글쓴이는 왜 이 문단을 "Conversely,"로 시작했나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: To signal the opposite case: buying more than selling (a deficit) instead of selling more than buying (a surplus).
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 파는 것보다 더 많이 사는 반대 상황(적자)을 알리기 위해서입니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: A deficit isn’t always bad.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: A deficit / isn’t always bad.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 적자는 / 항상 나쁜 것은 아니다.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 적자가 항상 나쁜 것만은 아니다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 부정어(isn’t) + always는 "절대 아니다"가 아니라 "늘 그런 것은 아니다"라는 균형 잡힌 부분부정입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: A trade deficit isn’t always bad for a country.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 축약형 isn’t(is not) + 빈도부사 always가 부분부정을 이룸니다. 5단어의 짧은 문장으로 오해를 바로잡는 핵심 문장입니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: The word "deficit" sounds negative, / so readers might worry. / This short sentence pauses / to correct that idea. / Having a trade deficit / is not always a bad thing.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: "적자"라는 단어가 부정적으로 들려 독자가 걱정할 수 있습니다. 이 짧은 문장은 그 오해를 바로잡습니다. 무역 적자를 갖는 것이 항상 나쁜 것만은 아닙니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Does "isn’t always bad" mean a deficit is never bad, or only not bad in every case?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: "isn’t always bad"는 적자가 절대 나쁘지 않다는 뜻인가요, 항상 나쁜 것만은 아니라는 뜻인가요?

teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 항상 나쁜 것만은 아니라는 부분부정입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Because people want them, or because countries don’t make enough of certain products at home.

sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 이름이 나타내듯, / 토이랜디아는 장난감 만들기를 전문으로 하고 / 스낵빌은 간식 만들기를 전문으로 한다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: If Toylandia sells toys worth $100 million to Snackville but only buys snacks worth $70 million, it has a trade surplus of $30 million.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: If Toylandia sells toys worth $100 million / to Snackville / but only buys snacks worth $70 million, / it has a trade surplus of $30 million.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 만약 토이랜디아가 1억 달러 가치의 장난감을 판다면 / 스낵빌에 / 하지만 7천만 달러 가치의 간식만 산다면, / 그 나라는 3천만 달러의 무역 흑자를 갖는다.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 만약 토이랜디아가 스낵빌에 1억 달러어치 장난감을 팔고 7천만 달러어치 간식만 사온다면, 토이랜디아는 3천만 달러의 무역 흑자를 기록한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 형용사 worth + 금액이 명사(toys / snacks) 뒤에서 가치를 수식합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Toylandia exported toys worth $100 million.

mustKnowChunks.use: $100 million(수출) − $70 million(수입) = $30 million(흑자) 산술 차액입니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Comparing $100 million and $70 million gives a surplus of $30 million.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 조건절 If + Toylandia sells ... but only buys ... 안에서 부사 only가 $70 million이 $100 million보다 적음을 강조합니다. 주절의 it은 Toylandia를 가리키며, $100 million − $70 million = $30 million 계산으로 흑자 금액이 나옵니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Look at the exact numbers / for Toylandia. / It earns $100 million by selling toys, / and spends only $70 million buying snacks. / Subtract $70 million from $100 million, / and Toylandia has a $30 million surplus.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: Toylandia의 정확한 숫자를 보세요. 장난감을 팔아 1억 달러($100 million)를 벌고, 간식을 사는 데 7천만 달러($70 million)만 썼습니다. $100 million에서 $70 million을 빼면 Toylandia는 $30 million의 무역 흑자를 갖게 됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Show the math: how do we get $30 million for Toylandia?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 계산을 보여 주세요. Toylandia의 $30 million은 어떻게 나오나요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: $100 million earned from selling toys minus $70 million spent buying snacks equals a $30 million surplus.
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 장난감 판매로 번 $100 million에서 간식 구매에 쓴 $70 million을 빼면 $30 million 흑자가 됩니다.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Snackville, on the other hand, has a trade deficit of $30 million because it buys more than it sells.
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Snackville, on the other hand, / has a trade deficit of $30 million / because it buys more than it sells.
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 스낵빌은, 반면에, / 3천만 달러의 무역 적자를 갖는다 / 파는 것보다 더 많이 사기 때문에.
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 반면 스낵빌은 파는 것보다 더 많이 사기 때문에 3천만 달러의 무역 적자를 기록한다.

mustKnowChunks.use: 주어 Snackville 뒤에 쌍쉼표(, on the other hand,)로 삽입되어 Toylandia와 대조합니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Toylandia has a surplus; Snackville, on the other hand, has a deficit.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: because it buys more than it sells
mustKnowChunks.meaning: 파는 것보다 더 많이 사기 때문에
mustKnowChunks.use: 이유 접속사 because가 적자의 원인($100M 구매 > $70M 판매)을 분명히 밝힙니다.
mustKnowChunks.example: Snackville has a $30 million deficit because it buys $100 million and sells $70 million.

sentenceAnalysis.mustKnowGrammar: 삽입 부사구 , on the other hand,가 주어 Snackville과 동사 has 사이에 들어가 앞 문장의 Toylandia와 정반대 결과를 대조합니다. 이유 절 because it buys more than it sells가 두 나라 사이 거래의 거울 구조($100M을 사고 $70M만 팔았음)를 완성합니다.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanation: Now look at the same trade / from Snackville’s side. / Snackville bought $100 million of toys / and sold $70 million of snacks. / Because it bought more than it sold, / Snackville has a $30 million trade deficit.
sentenceAnalysis.feynmanExplanationKo: 이제 같은 거래를 Snackville 입장에서 보세요. Snackville은 장난감 $100 million을 사고 간식 $70 million을 팔았습니다. 판 것보다 더 많이 샀기 때문에 Snackville은 $30 million의 무역 적자를 갖게 됩니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Teacher: Why are Toylandia’s surplus and Snackville’s deficit both $30 million?
teachingTranscript.korean: 교사: 왜 Toylandia의 흑자와 Snackville의 적자가 둘 다 $30 million인가요?

teachingTranscript.english: Student: Because they are trading with each other: Toylandia sells $100M and buys $70M (+$30M), while Snackville buys $100M and sells $70M (−$30M).
teachingTranscript.korean: 학생: 서로 거래하기 때문입니다. Toylandia는 $100M을 팔고 $70M을 사서 +$30M이고, Snackville은 $100M을 사고 $70M을 팔아 −$30M이 됩니다.

sentenceFrames: Attribution & Definitions: According to the article, exports are things a country sells to other countries, while imports are things a country buys from them.
Money Comparison: Countries keep track of how much money they earn from exports and spend on imports, and comparing these two numbers shows whether they have a trade surplus or a trade deficit.

Surplus vs. Deficit & Nuance: A trade surplus happens when a country sells more goods and services than it buys; conversely, a trade deficit occurs when it buys more than it sells, often because people want products or countries do not make enough at home.

Fictional Example: For example, fictional Toylandia sells toys worth $100 million to Snackville but buys only $70 million in snacks; therefore, Toylandia has a $30 million surplus, while Snackville has a $30 million deficit.
paragraphOutline: 1. Attribution & Definitions: Begin with "According to the article," and define exports (things a country sells) and imports (things a country buys).
2. Money Comparison: Explain that countries track money earned from exports and spent on imports, and compare the two numbers to identify a surplus or deficit.

3. Surplus vs. Deficit & Nuance: Define surplus ("sells more ... than it buys") vs. deficit ("buys more than it sells"), noting a deficit isn’t always bad because people want products or don’t make enough at home.
4. Fictional Toylandia–Snackville Example: End by showing Toylandia selling $100 million in toys and buying $70 million in snacks ($30 million surplus), while Snackville has a $30 million deficit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Exports are things a country buys, and imports are things a country sells.
commonMistakes.correction: Exports are things a country sells to another country, while imports are things a country buys from another country.
commonMistakes.explanation: Reversed definitions: ex- = out (sells) and im- = in (buys). Always verify against the two bullets under "What Is Trade?".

commonMistakes.mistake: A trade deficit is always bad for the economy and lowers GDP.
commonMistakes.correction: According to the article, a trade deficit isn’t always bad because people want imported things or countries don’t make enough of certain products at home.
commonMistakes.explanation: Outside macro claim & contradiction: the article explicitly states "A deficit isn’t always bad" and does not mention GDP or real-world macro policy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Toylandia sells $100 million and buys $70 million, so it has a $70 million surplus.
commonMistakes.correction: Toylandia sells toys worth $100 million to Snackville and buys snacks worth $70 million, giving Toylandia a trade surplus of $30 million.
commonMistakes.explanation: Arithmetic error: subtract imports ($70 million) from exports ($100 million) to get the $30 million difference.

commonMistakes.mistake: When a country sell more goods than it buy, it have a trade surplus.
commonMistakes.correction: When a country sells more goods and services than it buys, it has a trade surplus.
commonMistakes.explanation: Subject-verb agreement error: match singular subject "a country" / "it" with "sells," "buys," and "has."

teacherCorrectionFocus: Check word count (100–140 words) and exact prompt coverage: both definitions (imports & exports) and how countries identify surplus vs. deficit.
Verify opening source attribution ("According to the article,"), 3+ specific article details, comparison ("more ... than"), and cause/effect ("because," "therefore").
Confirm Toylandia and Snackville remain strictly fictional with exact dollar amounts ($100 million, $70 million, $30 million) and zero outside macroeconomic claims.
Check third-person singular "-s" ("a country sells / buys / has / specializes") and contrast connectors ("while," "conversely," "on the other hand").
finalWritingSupport.g1Scaffold: Provide G1 students the 4-step Paragraph Outline and sentence frames, guiding them to plug in "exports = sells," "imports = buys," "more ... than," "because," and exact Toylandia ($100M) / Snackville ($70M) / $30M numbers.
finalWritingSupport.g2Extension: Challenge G2 students to integrate "conversely" and "on the other hand" smoothly, include the article’s nuance that a deficit isn’t always bad ("at home"), and hit 115–130 words with zero factual drift.
